entries.330c0dff9d50d20d3b4238a7282716a55af80281: <div sID="gen13025" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="130" osisID="Ps.130" sID="Ps.130"/> <div eID="gen13025" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13026" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen13027" type="x-p"/> This psalm relates not to any temporal concern, either personal or public, but it is wholly taken up with the affairs of the soul. It is reckoned one of the seven penitential psalms, which have sometimes been made use of by penitents, upon their admission into the church; and, in singing it, we are all concerned to apply it to ourselves. The psalmist here expresses, I. His desire towards God, <reference osisRef="Ps.130.1-Ps.130.2">ver. 1, 2</reference>. II. His repentance before God, <reference osisRef="Ps.130.3-Ps.130.4">ver. 3, 4</reference>. III. His attendance upon God, <reference osisRef="Ps.130.5-Ps.130.6">ver. 5, 6</reference>. IV. His expectations from God, <reference osisRef="Ps.130.7-Ps.130.8">ver. 7, 8</reference>. And, as in water face answers to face, so does the heart of one humble penitent to another.
entries.a0ae1d735b150120f7cf2fa5419b6febde98de92: <div eID="gen13027" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen13026" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">God's Regard to His Church.</title> <div sID="gen13028" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Out of the depths have I cried unto thee, <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">2</hi> Lord, hear my voice: let thine ears be attentive to the voice of my supplications. <hi type="super">3</hi> If thou, <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , shouldest mark iniquities, O Lord, who shall stand? <hi type="super">4</hi> But <hi type="italic">there is</hi> forgiveness with thee, that thou mayest be feared. <div eID="gen13028" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13029" type="x-p"/> In these verses we are taught, <div eID="gen13029" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13030" type="x-p"/> I. Whatever condition we are in, though ever so deplorable, to continue calling upon God, <reference osisRef="Ps.130.1">v. 1</reference>. The best men may sometimes be in <hi type="italic">the depths,</hi> in great trouble and affliction, and utterly at a loss what to do, in the depths of distress and almost in the depths of despair, the spirit low and dark, sinking and drooping, cast down and disquieted. But, in the greatest depths, it is our privilege that we may cry unto God and be heard. A prayer may reach the heights of heaven, though not out of the depths of hell, yet out of the depths of the greatest trouble we can be in in this world, Jeremiah's out of the dungeon, Daniel's out of the den, and Jonah's out of the fish's belly. It is our duty and interest to cry unto God, for that is the likeliest way both to prevent our sinking lower and to recover us out of the <hi type="italic">horrible pit and miry clay,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.40.1-Ps.40.2">Ps. xl. 1, 2</reference>. <div eID="gen13030" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13031" type="x-p"/> II. While we continue calling upon God to assure ourselves of an answer of peace from him; for this is that which David in faith prays for (<reference osisRef="Ps.130.2">v. 2</reference>): <hi type="italic">Lord, hear my voice,</hi> my complaint and prayer, and <hi type="italic">let thy ears be attentive</hi> to the voice both of my afflictions and <hi type="italic">of my supplications.</hi> <div eID="gen13031" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13032" type="x-p"/> III. We are taught to humble ourselves before the justice of God as guilty in his sight, and unable to answer him for one of a thousand of our offences (<reference osisRef="Ps.130.3">v. 3</reference>): <hi type="italic">If thou, Lord, shouldst mark iniquities, O Lord! who shall stand?</hi> His calling God <hi type="italic">Lord</hi> twice, in so few words, <hi type="italic">Jah</hi> and <hi type="italic">Adonai,</hi> is very emphatic, and intimates a very awful sense of God's glorious majesty and a dread of his wrath. Let us learn here, 1. To acknowledge our iniquities, that we cannot justify ourselves before God, or plead Not guilty. There is that which is remarkable in our iniquities and is liable to be animadverted upon. 2. To own the power and justice of God, which are such that, if he were extreme to mark what we do amiss, there would be no hopes of coming off. His eye can discover enough in the best man to ground a condemnation upon; and, if he proceed against us, we have no way to help ourselves, we cannot stand, but shall certainly be cast. If God deal with us in strict justice, we are undone; if he make remarks upon our iniquities, he will find them to be many and great, greatly aggravated and very provoking; and then, if he should proceed accordingly, he would shut us out from all hope of his favour and shut us up under his wrath; and what could we do to help ourselves? We could not make our escape, nor resist not bear up under his avenging hand. 3. Let us admire God's patience and forbearance; we should be undone if he were to mark iniquities, and he knows it, and therefore bears with us. <hi type="italic">It is of his mercy that we are not consumed</hi> by his wrath. <div eID="gen13032" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13033" type="x-p"/> IV. We are taught to cast ourselves upon the pardoning mercy of God, and to comfort ourselves with that when we see ourselves obnoxious to his justice, <reference osisRef="Ps.130.4">v. 4</reference>. Here is, 1. God's grace discovered, and pleaded with him, by a penitent sinner: <hi type="italic">But there is forgiveness with thee.</hi> It is our unspeakable comfort, in all our approaches to God, that there is forgiveness with him, for that is what we need. He has put himself into a capacity to pardon sin; he has declared himself gracious and merciful, and ready to forgive, <reference osisRef="Exod.34.6-Exod.34.7">Exod. xxxiv. 6, 7</reference>. He has promised to forgive the sins of those that do repent. Never any that dealt with him found him implacable, but easy to be entreated, and swift to show mercy. With us there is iniquity, and therefore it is well for us that with him there is forgiveness. <hi type="italic">There is a propitiation with thee,</hi> so some read it. Jesus Christ is the great propitiation, the ransom which God has found; he is ever with him, as advocate for us, and through him we hope to obtain forgiveness. 2. Our duty designed in that discovery, and inferred from it: "<hi type="italic">There is forgiveness with thee,</hi> not that thou mayest be made bold with and presumed upon, but <hi type="italic">that thou mayest be feared</hi>—in general, that thou mayest be worshipped and served by the children of men, who, being sinners, could have no dealings with God, if he were not a Master that could pass by a great many faults." But this encourages us to come into his service that we shall not be turned off for every misdemeanour; no, nor for any, if we truly repent. This does in a special manner invite those who have sinned to repent, and return to the fear of God, that he is gracious and merciful, and will receive them upon their repentance, <reference osisRef="Joel.2.13">Joel ii. 13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.3.2">Matt. iii. 2</reference>. And, particularly, we are to have a holy awe and reverence of God's pardoning mercy (<reference osisRef="Hos.3.5">Hos. iii. 5</reference>, <hi type="italic">They shall fear the Lord, and his goodness</hi>); and <hi type="italic">then</hi> we may expect the benefit of the forgiveness that is with God when we make it the object of our holy fear.
entries.8984ffa6d5634b885b94281661fccd8d0a02ce27: <div eID="gen13033" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Encouragement to Trust in and Depend upon God.</title> <div sID="gen13034" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">5</hi> I wait for the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , my soul doth wait, and in his word do I hope. <hi type="super">6</hi> My soul <hi type="italic">waiteth</hi> for the Lord more than they that watch for the morning: <hi type="italic">I say, more than</hi> they that watch for the morning. <hi type="super">7</hi> Let Israel hope in the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> : for with the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> <hi type="italic">there is</hi> mercy, and with him <hi type="italic">is</hi> plenteous redemption. <hi type="super">8</hi> And he shall redeem Israel from all his iniquities. <div eID="gen13034" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13035" type="x-p"/> Here, I. The psalmist engages himself to trust in God and to wait for him, <reference osisRef="Ps.130.5-Ps.130.6">v. 5, 6</reference>. Observe, 1. His dependence upon God, expressed in a climax, it being a a song of degrees, or ascents: "<hi type="italic">I wait for the Lord;</hi> from him I expect relief and comfort, believing it will come, longing till it does come, but patiently bearing the delay of it, and resolving to look for it from no other hand. <hi type="italic">My soul doth wait;</hi> I wait for him in sincerity, and not in profession only. I am an expectant, and it is <hi type="italic">for the Lord</hi> that <hi type="italic">my soul waits,</hi> for the gifts of his grace and the operations of his power." 2. The ground of that dependence: <hi type="italic">In his word do I hope.</hi> We must hope for that only which he has promised in his word, and not for the creatures of our own fancy and imagination; we must hope for it because he has promised it, and not from any opinion of our own merit. 3. The degree of that dependence—"<hi type="italic">more than those that watch for the morning,</hi> who are, (1.) Well-assured that the morning will come; and so am I that God will return in mercy to me, according to his promise; for God's covenant is more firm than the ordinances of day and night, for they shall come to an end, but that is everlasting." (2.) Very desirous that it would come. Sentinels that keep guard upon the walls, those that watch with sick people, and travellers that are abroad upon their journey, long before day wish to see the dawning of the day; but more earnestly does this good man long for the tokens of God's favour and the visits of his grace, and more readily will he be aware of his first appearances than they are of day. Dr. Hammond reads it thus, <hi type="italic">My soul hastens to the Lord, from the guards in the morning, the guards in the morning,</hi> and gives this sense of it, "To thee I daily betake myself, early in the morning, addressing my prayers, and my very soul, before thee, at the time that the priests offer their morning sacrifice." <div eID="gen13035" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13036" type="x-p"/> II. He encourages all the people of God in like manner to depend upon him and trust in him: <hi type="italic">Let Israel hope in the Lord</hi> and <hi type="italic">wait for</hi> him; not only the body of the people, but every good man, who <hi type="italic">surnames himself by the name of Israel,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.44.5">Isa. xliv. 5</reference>. Let all that devote themselves to God cheerfully stay themselves upon him (<reference osisRef="Ps.130.7-Ps.130.8">v. 7, 8</reference>), for two reasons:—1. Because the light of nature discovers to us that <hi type="italic">there is mercy with him,</hi> that the God of Israel is a merciful God and <hi type="italic">the Father of mercies. Mercy is with</hi> him; not only inherent in his nature, but it is his delight, it is his darling attribute; it is with him in all his works, in all his counsels. 2. Because the light of the gospel discovers to us that <hi type="italic">there is redemption with him,</hi> contrived by him, and to be wrought out <hi type="italic">in the fulness of time;</hi> it was in the beginning hidden in God. See here, (1.) The nature of this redemption; it is redemption from sin, from all sin, and therefore can be no other than that eternal redemption which Jesus Christ became the author of; for it is he <hi type="italic">that saves his people from their sins</hi> (<reference osisRef="Matt.1.21">Matt. i. 21</reference>), that <hi type="italic">redeems them from all iniquity</hi> (<reference osisRef="Titus.2.14">Tit. ii. 14</reference>), and <hi type="italic">turns away ungodliness from Jacob,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.11.26">Rom. xi. 26</reference>. It is he that redeems us both from the condemning and from the commanding power of sin. (2.) The riches of this redemption; it <hi type="italic">is plenteous redemption;</hi> there is an all-sufficient fulness of merit and grace in the Redeemer, enough for all, enough for each; enough for me, says the believer. Redemption from sin includes redemption from all other evils, and therefore is a plenteous redemption. (3.) The persons to whom the benefits of this redemption belong: <hi type="italic">He shall redeem Israel,</hi> Israel according to the spirit, all those who are in covenant with God, as Israel was, and who are <hi type="italic">Israelites indeed, in whom is no guile.</hi>  <chapter eID="Ps.130"/> <div eID="gen13036" type="x-p"/>

entries.8c78aa2112461c95249d408411e29cfbc73f416f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv7032"/><title type="x-s2">PSALM 130</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Ps.130.1-Ps.130.8">Psa 130:1-8</reference>. The penitent sinner's hope is in God's mercy only.</title> <div sID="gen10787" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv7032"/><hi type="bold">1-2. depths--</hi>for great distress (<reference osisRef="Ps.40.2">Psa 40:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.69.3">69:3</reference>). <div eID="gen10787" type="x-p"/>
entries.a78439c5b0987a1877066c775e101c1f5face571: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv7033"/><div sID="gen10788" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv7033"/><hi type="bold">3. shouldest mark--</hi>or, "take strict account" (<reference osisRef="Job.10.14">Job 10:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.14.16">14:16</reference>), implying a confession of the existence of sin.<div eID="gen10788" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10789" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">who shall stand--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ps.1.6">Psa 1:6</reference>). Standing is opposed to the guilty sinking down in fear and self-condemnation (Mal 3:2; <reference osisRef="Rev.6.15">Re 6:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rev.6.16">16</reference>). The question implies a negative, which is thus more strongly stated. <div eID="gen10789" type="x-p"/>
entries.423f653dda3432ff86c37d2188fa5f6e03b25ff6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv7034"/><div sID="gen10790" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv7034"/>4. Pardon produces filial fear and love. Judgment without the hope of pardon creates fear and dislike. The sense of forgiveness, so far from producing licentiousness, produces holiness (<reference osisRef="Jer.33.9">Jr 33:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.16.62">Eze 16:62</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.16.63">63</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Pet.2.16">1Pe 2:16</reference>). "There is forgiveness with thee, not that thou mayest be presumed upon, but feared." <div eID="gen10790" type="x-p"/>
entries.0edc7292db138f3d7b6b95f36acc465f3399abe0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv7035"/><div sID="gen10791" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv7035"/><hi type="bold">5-6. wait for the Lord--</hi>in expectation (<reference osisRef="Ps.27.14">Psa 27:14</reference>).<div eID="gen10791" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10792" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">watch for, &c.--</hi>in earnestness and anxiety. <div eID="gen10792" type="x-p"/>
entries.60e982fee5048ac2eb9624c3247e4615c8857449: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv7036"/><div sID="gen10793" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv7036"/><hi type="bold">7-8. Let Israel, &c.--</hi>that is, All are invited to seek and share divine forgiveness.<div eID="gen10793" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10794" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">from all his iniquities--</hi>or, "punishments of them" (<reference osisRef="Ps.40.12">Psa 40:12</reference>, &c.). <chapter eID="Ps.130"/>

entries.9d9789afe0b007a81acec204b02e501c9120efcf: <div eID="gen23149" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen23150" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen23151" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen23151" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen23150" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen23152" type="x-p"/> The prayer of a penitent to God, with confession of sin, <reference osisRef="Psa.130.1-Psa.130.3">Psa 130:1-3</reference>. Confidence in God's mercy, and waiting upon him, <reference osisRef="Psa.130.4-Psa.130.6">Psa 130:4-6</reference>. Israel is encouraged to hope in the Lord, because of his willingness to save, <reference osisRef="Psa.130.7">Psa 130:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.130.8">Psa 130:8</reference>. <div eID="gen23152" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23153" type="x-p"/> This Psalm has no title nor author's name, either in the Hebrew, or in any of the Versions; though the Syriac says it was spoken of Nehemiah the priest. It was most probably composed during the captivity; and contains the complaint of the afflicted Jews, with their hopes of the remission of those sins which were the cause of their sufferings, and their restoration from captivity to their own land. This is one of those called penitential Psalms. <div eID="gen23153" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23154" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen23154" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23155" type="x-p"/> Out of the depths - The captives in Babylon represent their condition like those who are in a prison - an abyss or deep ditch, ready to be swallowed up.
entries.ba46a7ec5f4d9c0822e72ffe1a3610981a2b1443: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen23155" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23156" type="x-p"/> Lord, hear my voice - They could have no helper but God, and to him they earnestly seek for relief.
entries.f9e0be971bd08b7dd60704b7aba5f0560718d880: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen23156" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23157" type="x-p"/> If thou - shouldest mark iniquities - If thou shouldst set down every deviation in thought, word, and deed from thy holy law; and if thou shouldst call us into judgment for all our infidelities, both of heart and life; O Lord, who could stand? Who could stand such a trial, and who could stand acquitted in the judgment? This is a most solemn saying; and if we had not the doctrine that is in the next verse, who could be saved?
entries.8f6f7334d559e7318d1e7cf1e79e3d71a989973b: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen23157" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23158" type="x-p"/> But there is forgiveness with thee - Thou canst forgive; mercy belongs to thee, as well as judgment. The doctrine here is the doctrine of St. John: "If any man sin, we have an Advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous; and he is the propitiation for our sins, and not for ours only, but also for the sins of the whole world." "Hear, O heavens, and give ear, O earth; for the Lord hath spoken!" Jesus has died for our sins; therefore God can be just, and yet the justifier of him who believeth in Jesus.
entries.d38ddea1d4fcda35d1c5d6f50dc37f41edfb91f8: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen23158" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23159" type="x-p"/> I wait for the Lord - The word קוה kavah, which we translate to wait, properly signifies the extension of a cord from one point to another. This is a fine metaphor: God is one point, the human heart is the other; and the extended cord between both is the earnest believing desire of the soul. This desire, strongly extended from the heart to God, in every mean of grace, and when there is none, is the active, energetic waiting which God requires, and which will be successful.
entries.c2bdcd723c62d243a4c5fadecd03ac11706b82e6: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen23159" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23160" type="x-p"/> More than they that watch for the morning - I believe the original should be read differently from what it is here. The Chaldee has, "More than they who observe the morning watches, that they may offer the morning oblation." This gives a good sense, and is, perhaps, the true meaning. Most of the Versions have "From the morning to the night watches." Or the passage may be rendered, "My soul waiteth for the Lord from the morning watches to the morning watches." That is, "I wait both day and night."
entries.df1f1f3cbce4a001887de21a29532e66fa12ebfc: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen23160" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23161" type="x-p"/> Let Israel hope in the Lord - This, to hope for salvation, is their duty and their interest. But what reason is there for this hope? A twofold reason: - <div eID="gen23161" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23162" type="x-p"/> 1. With the Lord there is mercy - החסד hachesed, That mercy, the fund, the essence of mercy. <div eID="gen23162" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23163" type="x-p"/> 2. And with him is plenteous redemption - והרבה עמו פדות veharabbah immo peduth; and that abundant redemption, that to which there is none like, the Fountain of redemption, the Lamb of God which taketh away the sin of the world. The article ה, both in הרבה harabbah and החסד hachesed, is very emphatic.
entries.1cee6bda099eb194c169dc25c0b2db4eccc905db: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen23163" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23164" type="x-p"/> He shall redeem Israel - Και αυτος υτρωσει, "He will make a ransom for Israel," He will provide a great price for Israel, and by it will take away all his iniquities. I would not restrict this to Israel in Babylon. Every believer may take it to himself. God perfectly justifies and perfectly sanctifies all that come unto him through the Son of his love.  <chapter eID="Ps.130"/> <div eID="gen23164" type="x-p"/>

entries.8346baa7cc996e2babd0acbe530447a920e2cdac: <div eID="gen10213" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s2">De Profundis</title> <div sID="gen10214" type="x-p"/> Luther, being once asked which were the best Psalms, replied, <hi type="italic">Psalmi Paulini</hi>; and when his companions at table pressed him to say which these were, he answered: <reference osisRef="Ps.32.1-Ps.32.11">Psa 32:1-11</reference>; Ps 51; <reference osisRef="Ps.130.1-Ps.130.8">Psa 130:1-8</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Ps.143.1">Psa 143:1</reference>-12. In fact in <reference osisRef="Ps.130.1-Ps.130.8">Psa 130:1-8</reference> the condemnability of the natural man, the freeness of mercy, and the spiritual nature of redemption are expressed in a manner thoroughly Pauline. It is the sixth among the seven <hi type="italic">Psalmi poenitentiales</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.6.1-Ps.6.10">Psa 6:1-10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.32.1-Ps.32.11">Psa 32:1-11</reference>, Ps 38, Ps 51, Ps 102, <reference osisRef="Ps.130.1-Ps.130.8">Psa 130:1-8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.143.1-Ps.143.12">Psa 143:1-12</reference>). <div eID="gen10214" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10215" type="x-p"/> Even the chronicler had this Psalm before him in the present classification, which puts it near to Ps 132; ; for the independent addition with which he enriches Solomon’s prayer at the dedication of the Temple, <reference osisRef="2Chr.6.40-2Chr.6.42">2Ch 6:40-42</reference>, is compiled out of passages of <reference osisRef="Ps.130.1-Ps.130.8">Psa 130:1-8</reference> (<reference osisRef="Ps.130.2">Psa 130:2</reference>, cf. the divine response, <reference osisRef="2Chr.7.15">2Ch 7:15</reference>) and Ps 132 (<reference osisRef="Ps.132.8">Psa 132:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.132.16">Psa 132:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.132.10">Psa 132:10</reference>). <div eID="gen10215" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10216" type="x-p"/> The mutual relation of <reference osisRef="Ps.130.1-Ps.130.8">Psa 130:1-8</reference> to Ps 86 has been already noticed there. The two Psalms are first attempts at adding a third, Adonajic style to the Jehovic and Elohimic Psalm-style. There <hi type="italic">Adonaj</hi> is repeated seven times, and three times in this Psalm. There are also other indications that the writer of <reference osisRef="Ps.130.1-Ps.130.8">Psa 130:1-8</reference> was acquainted with that Ps 86 (compare <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.130.2">Psa 130:2</reference></hi>, שׁמעה בקולי, with <reference osisRef="Ps.86.6">Psa 86:6</reference>, והקשׁיבה בּקול; <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.130.2">Psa 130:2</reference></hi>, לקול תּחנוּני, with <reference osisRef="Ps.86.6">Psa 86:6</reference>, בּקול תּחנוּנותי; <reference osisRef="Ps.130.4">Psa 130:4</reference>, עמּך הסּליחה, with <reference osisRef="Ps.86.5">Psa 86:5</reference>, וסלּח; <reference osisRef="Ps.130.8">Psa 130:8</reference>, החסד עם ה/ הח, with <reference osisRef="Ps.86.5">Psa 86:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.86.15">Psa 86:15</reference>, רב־חסד). The fact that קשּׁוּב (after the form שׁכּוּל), occurs besides only in those dependent passages of the chronicler, and קשּׁב only in <reference osisRef="Neh.1.6">Neh 1:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Neh.1.11">Neh 1:11</reference>, as סליחה besides only in <reference osisRef="Dan.9.9">Dan 9:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Neh.9.17">Neh 9:17</reference>, brings our Psalm down into a later period of the language; and moreover Ps 86 is not Davidic.
entries.8ce4cf191c4eba180fe93b9ecdc46a5f0f9adeee: <reference osisRef="Ps.130.1-Ps.130.4">Psa 130:1-4</reference> <div eID="gen10216" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10217" type="x-p"/> The depths (מעמקּים) are not the depths of the soul, but the deep outward and inward distress in which the poet is sunk as in deep waters (<reference osisRef="Ps.69.3">Psa 69:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.69.15">Psa 69:15</reference>). Out of these depths he cries to the God of salvation, and importunately prays Him who rules all things and can do all things to grant him a compliant hearing (שׁמע בּ, <reference osisRef="Gen.21.12">Gen 21:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.26.13">Gen 26:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.30.6">Gen 30:6</reference>, and other passages). God heard indeed even in Himself, as being the omniscient One, the softest and most secret as well as the loudest utterance; but, as Hilary observes, <hi type="italic">fides officium suum exsequitur, ut Dei auditionem roget, ut qui per naturam suam audit per orantis precem dignetur audire</hi>. In this sense the poet prays that His ears may be turned קשּׁבות (duller collateral form of קשּׁב, to be in the condition of <hi type="italic">arrectae aures</hi>), with strained attention, to his loud and urgent petition (<reference osisRef="Ps.28.2">Psa 28:2</reference>). His life hangs upon the thread of the divine compassion. If God preserves iniquities, who can stand before Him?! He preserves them (שׁמר) when He puts them down to one (<reference osisRef="Ps.32.2">Psa 32:2</reference>) and keeps them in remembrance (<reference osisRef="Gen.37.11">Gen 37:11</reference>), or, as it is figuratively expressed in <reference osisRef="Job.14.17">Job 14:17</reference>, sealed up as it were in custody in order to punish them when the measure is full. The inevitable consequence of this is the destruction of the sinner, for nothing can stand against the punitive justice of God (<reference osisRef="Nah.1.6">Nah 1:6</reference>; Mal 3:2; Ezr 9:15). If God should show Himself as <hi type="italic">Jāh</hi>,<note placement="foot">Eusebius on Ps 68 (67):<reference osisRef="Ps.68.5">5</reference> observes that the Logos is called Ἴα as μορφὴν δούλον λαβὼν καὶ τάς ἀκτῖνας τῆς ἑαυτοῦ θεότητος συστείλας καὶ ὥσπερ καταδὺς ἐν τῷ σώματι. There is a similar passage in Vicentius Ciconia (1567), which we introduced into our larger Commentary on the Psalms (1859-60).</note> no creature would be able to stand before Him, who is <hi type="italic">Adonaj</hi>, and can therefore carry out His judicial will or purpose (<reference osisRef="Isa.51.16">Isa 51:16</reference>). He does not, however, act thus. He does not proceed according to the legal stringency of recompensative justice. This thought, which fills up the pause after the question, but is not directly expressed, is confirmed by the following כּי, which therefore, as in <reference osisRef="Job.22.2">Job 22:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.31.18">Job 31:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.39.14">Job 39:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.28.28">Isa 28:28</reference> (cf. <reference osisRef="Eccl.5.6">Ecc 5:6</reference>), introduces the opposite. With the Lord is the willingness to forgive (הסּליחה), in order that He may be feared; i.e., He forgives, as it is expressed elsewhere (e.g., <reference osisRef="Ps.79.9">Psa 79:9</reference>), for His Name’s sake: He seeks therein the glorifying of His Name. He will, as the sole Author of our salvation, who, putting all vain-glorying to shame, causes mercy instead of justice to take its course with us (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.51.6">Psa 51:6</reference>), be reverenced; and gives the sinner occasion, ground, and material for reverential thanksgiving and praise by bestowing “forgiveness” upon him in the plenitude of absolutely free grace.
entries.e8d266907101c84c70fa9c8fb2338f5999c3c27a: <reference osisRef="Ps.130.5-Ps.130.8">Psa 130:5-8</reference> <div eID="gen10217" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10218" type="x-p"/> Therefore the sinner need not, therefore too the poet will not, despair. He hopes in Jahve (<hi type="italic">acc. obj.</hi> as in <reference osisRef="Ps.25.5">Psa 25:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.25.21">Psa 25:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.40.2">Psa 40:2</reference>), his soul hopes; hoping in and waiting upon God is the mood of his inmost and of his whole being. He waits upon God’s word, the word of His salvation (<reference osisRef="Ps.119.81">Psa 119:81</reference>), which, if it penetrates into the soul and cleaves there, calms all unrest, and by the appropriated consolation of forgiveness transforms and enlightens for it everything in it and outside of it. His soul is לאדני, i.e., stedfastly and continually directed towards Him; as Chr. A. Crusius when on his death-bed, with hands and eyes uplifted to heaven, joyfully exclaimed: “My soul is full of the mercy of Jesus Christ. <hi type="italic">My whole soul is towards God.</hi>” The meaning of לאדני becomes at once clear in itself from <reference osisRef="Ps.143.6">Psa 143:6</reference>, and is defined moreover, without supplying שׁמרת (Hitzig), according to the following לבּקר. Towards the Lord he is expectantly turned, like those who in the night-time wait for the morning. The repetition of the expression “those who watch for the morning” (cf. <reference osisRef="Isa.21.11">Isa 21:11</reference>) gives the impression of protracted, painful waiting. The wrath, in the sphere of which the poet now finds himself, is a nightly darkness, out of which he wishes to be removed into the sunny realm of love (Mal 4:2); not he alone, however, but at the same time all Israel, whose need is the same, and for whom therefore believing waiting is likewise the way to salvation. With Jahve, and with Him exclusively, with Him, however, also in all its fulness, is החסד (contrary to Ps 62:13, without any pausal change in accordance with the varying of the segolates), the mercy, which removes the guilt of sin and its consequences, and puts freedom, peace, and joy into the heart. And plenteous (הרבּה, an adverbial <hi type="italic">infin. absol.</hi>, used here, as in <reference osisRef="Ezek.21.20">Eze 21:20</reference>, as an adjective) is with Him redemption; i.e., He possesses in the richest measure the willingness, the power, and the wisdom, which are needed to procure redemption, which rises up as a wall of partition (<reference osisRef="Exod.8.19">Exo 8:19</reference>) between destruction and those imperilled. To Him, therefore, must the individual, if he will obtain mercy, to Him must His people, look up hopingly; and this hope directed to Him shall not be put to shame: He, in the fulness of the might of His free grace (<reference osisRef="Isa.43.25">Isa 43:25</reference>), will redeem Israel from all its iniquities, by forgiving them and removing their unhappy inward and outward consequences. With this promise (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.25.22">Psa 25:22</reference>) the poet comforts himself. He means complete and final redemption, above all, in the genuinely New Testament manner, spiritual redemption.  <chapter eID="Ps.130"/> <div eID="gen10218" type="x-p"/>

entries.25668844001cdf9821458126a4166096a82e2588:
PSALM 130
Whether the Prophet in this Psalm prays in his own name in particular, or represents the whole Church, it is manifest, that finding himself overwhelmed with adversities, he supplicates deliverance with passionate ardor. And while acknowledging that he is justly chastised by the hand of God, he encourages himself and all genuine believers to cherish good hope, since God is the everlasting deliverer of his people, and has always in readiness the means of effecting their rescue from death.
A Song of Degrees.
Psalm 130:1-4
1. Out of the deep places have I cried to thee, O Jehovah 2. O Lord hear voice; let thine ears be attentive to the voice of my prayers 3. If thou, O God shouldst mark iniquities, O Lord who shall stand? 4. But with thee there is forgiveness that thou mayest be feared.
 
1. Out of the deep places have I cried to thee, O Jehovah! It is to be noticed that the Prophet speaks of himself as sending forth his voice, as it were from out of a deep gulf,
The depths or deep gulfs are used in Scripture as an emblem of extreme danger or calamity, whether of body or of mind. See Psalm 69:2, 15. “The Papists, taking the deep as a type of purgatory, recite this Psalm in the persons of those who have died in their communion.” — Cresswell. To this Calvin afterwards adverts.
feeling himself overwhelmed with calamities. As the miseries to which there is no prospect of a termination commonly bring despair in their train, nothing is more difficult than for persons, when involved in grievous and deep sorrow, to stir up their minds to the exercise of prayer. And it is wonderful, considering that whilst we enjoy peace and prosperity we are cold in prayer, (because then our hearts are in a state of infatuated security, how in adversities, which ought to quicken us, we are still more stupefied. But the Prophet derives confidence in coming to the time one of grace from the very troubles, cares, dangers and sorrow into which he was plunged. He expresses his perplexity and the earnestness of his desire both by the word cry, and by the repetition continued in the second verse. So much the more detestable then is the barbarous ignorance of the Papist’s, in shamefully profaning this Psalm by wresting; it to a purpose wholly foreign to its genuine application. To what intent do they mumble it over for the dead, if it; is not that, in consequence of Satan having bewitched them, they may by their profanity extinguish a doctrine of singular utility? From the time that this Psalm was, by, a forced interpretation, applied to the souls of the dead, it is very generally believed to be of no use whatever to the living, and thus the world has lost an inestimable treasure.
